history.q: At the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE, Athenians defeated an invading army from which empire?
history.fact: The legend of a messenger running from Marathon to Athens inspired the marathon race, first run at the 1896 Athens Olympics.

history.q: Which Macedonian king built an empire stretching from Greece to India?
history.fact: Tutored as a teenager by Aristotle, Alexander founded many cities bearing his name, most famously Alexandria in Egypt.

history.q: Which Spartan king led the Greek stand at Thermopylae in 480 BCE?
history.fact: The famous 300 Spartans fought alongside thousands of other Greeks, including about 700 Thespians who also stayed to the end.

history.q: During the Peloponnesian War (431-404 BCE), which city-state led the alliance that fought Athens?
history.fact: The war's great chronicler, Thucydides, was himself an Athenian general who was exiled after a military failure.

history.q: In which year did the Greek War of Independence against the Ottoman Empire begin?
history.fact: Greece celebrates Independence Day on 25 March, the same day as the Orthodox Feast of the Annunciation.

history.q: The Bronze Age Minoan civilisation was centred on which island?
history.fact: The palace of Knossos, excavated by Arthur Evans from 1900, is linked in legend to the Minotaur's labyrinth.

history.q: In which year did Constantinople, capital of the Byzantine Empire, fall to the Ottomans?
history.fact: The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, died defending the city's walls on 29 May 1453.

history.q: Which Athenian statesman masterminded the Greek naval victory at Salamis in 480 BCE?
history.fact: Themistocles had earlier persuaded Athens to spend a windfall from its Laurion silver mines on building a fleet of warships.

history.q: Which 1827 naval battle, won by British, French and Russian fleets, proved decisive for Greek independence?
history.fact: Fought off modern Pylos, Navarino was the last major naval battle fought entirely with wooden sailing ships.

history.q: Which town served as Greece's capital before the seat of government moved to Athens in 1834?
history.fact: Ioannis Kapodistrias, independent Greece's first head of state, was assassinated outside a church in Nafplio in 1831.

technology.q: Which Greek mathematician of Syracuse is said to have shouted 'Eureka!' in his bath?
technology.fact: Archimedes also designed war machines to defend Syracuse against a Roman siege, which ended with his death in 212 BCE.

technology.q: Which ancient Greek physician is known as the 'father of medicine'?
technology.fact: Hippocrates came from the island of Kos and taught that diseases have natural causes rather than being punishments from the gods.

technology.q: Which Greek thinker gives his name to the theorem a² + b² = c²?
technology.fact: Pythagoras was born on the island of Samos, where the harbour town of Pythagoreio now bears his name.

technology.q: Which Greek mathematician wrote the 'Elements', the classic textbook of geometry?
technology.fact: Euclid worked in Alexandria around 300 BCE; his Elements served as the standard geometry textbook for over 2,000 years.

technology.q: The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from an ancient shipwreck in 1901, was used for what?
choices: Measuring the depth of the sea
technology.fact: Often called the world's first analogue computer, its corroded bronze gears are displayed at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

technology.q: Which Greek scholar estimated the Earth's circumference using shadows cast in two Egyptian cities?
technology.fact: Eratosthenes, chief librarian at Alexandria, is also credited with coining the word 'geography'.

technology.q: Hero of Alexandria described the aeolipile, a spinning sphere driven by what?
technology.fact: Hero also described a coin-operated holy-water dispenser, often called the world's first vending machine.

technology.q: Which ancient Greek astronomer is credited with the earliest known model placing the Sun at the centre of the cosmos?
technology.fact: Aristarchus also tried to measure the sizes and distances of the Sun and Moon, concluding the Sun was much larger than the Earth.

technology.q: Opened in 1893, the Corinth Canal links the Gulf of Corinth with which other gulf?
technology.fact: About 6.4 km long and only about 21 m wide at water level, the canal realised a project first attempted by Emperor Nero in 67 CE.

technology.q: Greek-born physician Georgios Papanikolaou pioneered a screening test for which disease?
technology.fact: Born in Kymi on the island of Euboea, Papanikolaou did his research in New York; his 'Pap test' has saved countless lives.

art.q: Who is traditionally credited as the author of the 'Iliad' and the 'Odyssey'?
art.fact: The Iliad is set during the Trojan War, while the Odyssey follows Odysseus' ten-year voyage home to Ithaca.

art.q: To which goddess was the Parthenon in Athens dedicated?
art.fact: Built in 447-432 BCE, the Parthenon was badly damaged in 1687 when a Venetian shell ignited Ottoman gunpowder stored inside.

art.q: The Venus de Milo statue, now in the Louvre, was found on which Greek island?
art.fact: Found by a farmer in 1820, the statue is thought to depict Aphrodite; her missing arms have never been found.

art.q: Which Greek-American soprano was nicknamed 'La Divina'?
art.fact: Born in New York to Greek parents, Callas spent her teenage years in Athens, where she trained at the conservatory.

art.q: Which Athenian playwright wrote the tragedy 'Oedipus Rex'?
art.fact: Sophocles is said to have written over 120 plays, but only seven complete tragedies survive.

art.q: The painter El Greco, famous for his work in Toledo, Spain, was born on which island?
art.fact: His real name was Domenikos Theotokopoulos; 'El Greco' simply means 'the Greek' in Spanish.

art.q: Which order of classical columns, the plainest of the three Greek orders, was used for the Parthenon's outer colonnade?
art.fact: The Parthenon's columns swell slightly in the middle, a technique called entasis that makes them look perfectly straight from afar.

art.q: Which ancient theatre in the Peloponnese is famed for acoustics so good that a whisper on stage carries to the back rows?
art.fact: Built in the 4th century BCE and seating around 14,000, the theatre still hosts plays every summer during the Epidaurus Festival.

art.q: Which Cretan author wrote the novel 'Zorba the Greek'?
art.fact: Kazantzakis' grave in Heraklion bears the epitaph: 'I hope for nothing. I fear nothing. I am free.'

art.q: Who became the first Greek to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1963?
art.fact: Seferis was also a career diplomat who served as Greek ambassador in London; Odysseas Elytis became Greece's second literature laureate in 1979.

politics.q: Democracy, meaning 'rule by the people', first developed in which ancient city-state?
politics.fact: Athenian citizens voted directly on laws in the Assembly, which met on the Pnyx hill facing the Acropolis.

politics.q: Which Athenian statesman led the city in its 5th-century BCE 'Golden Age' and championed building the Parthenon?
politics.fact: Pericles' famous Funeral Oration was recorded by the historian Thucydides; Pericles died during the plague of Athens in 429 BCE.

politics.q: In ancient Athens, what was the practice of voting to exile a citizen for ten years called?
politics.fact: Voters scratched names on pottery shards called ostraka; thousands of these have been excavated in Athens.

politics.q: Under its 1975 constitution, what is Greece's form of government?
politics.fact: Greece's president is elected by Parliament and is largely ceremonial; executive power lies with the Prime Minister and cabinet.

politics.q: Whose reforms of 508/507 BCE are traditionally seen as founding Athenian democracy?
politics.fact: Cleisthenes reorganised Athenian citizens into ten new tribes, breaking the power of old aristocratic clans.

politics.q: A military junta known as 'the Colonels' ruled Greece from 1967 until which year?
politics.fact: Greeks commemorate the November 1973 Athens Polytechnic uprising against the junta every year on 17 November.

politics.q: How many members sit in Greece's single-chamber Hellenic Parliament?
politics.fact: Parliament meets in the Old Royal Palace on Syntagma Square, originally built for King Otto.

politics.q: In which year did Greece join the European Economic Community?
politics.fact: Greece became the EEC's tenth member on 1 January 1981, five years before Spain and Portugal joined.

politics.q: Who was the last King of Greece, before the monarchy was abolished by referendum in 1974?
politics.fact: Before becoming king, Constantine won an Olympic gold medal in sailing at the 1960 Rome Games.

politics.q: Otto, the first king of modern Greece, was a prince from which German kingdom?
politics.fact: Otto arrived in Greece in 1833 aged just 17; he was deposed in 1862 and returned to Bavaria.

current-affairs.q: Which party won Greece's June 2023 parliamentary election outright?
current-affairs.fact: Kyriakos Mitsotakis, whose father Konstantinos was Prime Minister in 1990-93, began a second term as Prime Minister after the vote.

current-affairs.q: Greek basketball star Giannis Antetokounmpo won the 2021 NBA championship with which team?
current-affairs.fact: Born in Athens to Nigerian parents, Giannis scored 50 points in the title-clinching game and was named Finals MVP.

current-affairs.q: In April 2024, the Olympic flame was lit at Ancient Olympia for which Summer Games?
current-affairs.fact: The flame sailed from Greece to Marseille aboard the Belem, a three-masted ship built in the 19th century.

current-affairs.q: Which Greek city opened its long-awaited metro system in November 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Construction was slowed for years by spectacular Byzantine and Roman finds, some of which are now displayed inside the stations.

current-affairs.q: Who became Greece's first female President in March 2020?
current-affairs.fact: Sakellaropoulou, a judge, had previously been the first woman to lead Greece's Council of State, its supreme administrative court.

current-affairs.q: Which former Prime Minister stepped down as leader of SYRIZA after the 2023 elections?
current-affairs.fact: Tsipras became Prime Minister in January 2015 aged 40 and steered Greece through that summer's dramatic bailout referendum.

current-affairs.q: In 2024, which club became the first Greek side to win a major UEFA club trophy, the Europa Conference League?
current-affairs.fact: Olympiacos beat Fiorentina 1-0 in extra time, and the final happened to be played in Athens.

current-affairs.q: In February 2024, Greece became the first Orthodox Christian-majority country to legalise what?
current-affairs.fact: The same law also gave same-sex married couples the right to adopt children.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected President of Greece by Parliament in February 2025?
current-affairs.fact: Tasoulas had served as Speaker of the Hellenic Parliament before taking up the presidency in March 2025.

current-affairs.q: Miltiadis Tentoglou won Olympic gold at both Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 in which event?
current-affairs.fact: In Tokyo he tied Cuba's Juan Miguel Echevarría at 8.41 m with his final jump and took gold thanks to a better second-best leap.

general.q: Which mountain, the highest in Greece, was said to be the home of the gods?
general.fact: Olympus' highest peak, Mytikas, rises to about 2,918 m and was first climbed only in 1913.

general.q: Which sea lies between mainland Greece and Turkey?
general.fact: In myth, the Aegean takes its name from King Aegeus of Athens, who threw himself into the sea believing his son Theseus was dead.

general.q: The word 'alphabet' comes from 'alpha' plus which other Greek letter?
general.fact: Adapted from Phoenician script, the Greek alphabet was the first to use separate letters for vowels.

general.q: Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
general.fact: Spyridon Louis, a Greek water-carrier, won the 1896 marathon and became a national hero.

general.q: In 2004, Greece's men's football team stunned Europe by winning which tournament?
general.fact: Greece beat hosts Portugal 1-0 in the Lisbon final, thanks to a header by Angelos Charisteas.

general.q: Which self-governing peninsula in northern Greece is home to 20 Orthodox monasteries?
general.fact: Women have been barred from Mount Athos for over a thousand years, under a rule known as the avaton.

general.q: The whitewashed villages of Oia and Fira perch on the volcanic caldera of which island?
general.fact: Santorini's huge Bronze Age eruption (c. 1600 BCE) buried the town of Akrotiri, preserving it like a Greek Pompeii.

general.q: Feta cheese is traditionally made mainly from which milk?
general.fact: Since 2002, 'feta' has been an EU Protected Designation of Origin: only brined cheese from designated parts of Greece may use the name.

general.q: How many horizontal stripes are on the flag of Greece?
general.fact: The nine blue and white stripes are popularly said to stand for the syllables of 'Eleftheria i Thanatos' ('Freedom or Death').

general.q: What is the longest river flowing entirely within Greece?
general.fact: About 300 km long, the Aliakmonas runs from the Pindus mountains to the Thermaic Gulf near Thessaloniki.
